docs.title: German sentence patterns that show through
docs.text:
These are not vocabulary errors. Every word is English and the sentence still sounds German.

Pattern Sounds German Say instead Verb second after an adverbial Yesterday went I to the library. Yesterday I went to the library. Verb at the end of a subordinate clause … because he the answer knew. … because he knew the answer. Since for a period I live here since three years. I have lived here for three years. Until for a deadline I finish it until Friday. I will finish it by Friday. Make for do I have to make my homework. I have to do my homework. Become for get He became a present. He got a present. Missing do in questions Know you the answer? Do you know the answer? Information as a plural The informations are helpful. The information is helpful. Article with abstract nouns The life is difficult. Life is difficult. Also for so Also, we decided to leave. So we decided to leave. Actually for currently Actually he lives in Leeds. At present he lives in Leeds. Present for future after if If it will rain, we stay in. If it rains, we will stay in. Comma before that He said, that he was late. He said that he was late. In the year 2020 In the year 2020 the law changed. In 2020 the law changed. Double negative from nicht mehr He does not work not anymore. He no longer works there.

docs.title: Small words that give you away
docs.text: Confusion The rule in one line since / for Since takes a point in time, for takes a stretch of time its / it's It's is only ever it is or it has who / which Who for people, which for things, that for either in defining clauses fewer / less Fewer for things you can count, less for things you cannot each other / one another Interchangeable in modern English. Do not agonize economic / economical Economic relates to the economy, economical means thrifty historic / historical Historic means important, historical means from the past effect / affect Effect is nearly always the noun, affect the verb lay / lie You lie down, you lay something down borrow / lend You borrow from, you lend to say / tell You say something, you tell someone learn / teach Students learn, teachers teach

docs.title: Punctuation, briefly
docs.text:
German comma rules do not transfer. Three that turn up constantly:

  • No comma before that. He argued that the law was unfair.
  • A comma before a non-defining relative clause, none before a defining one. My brother, who lives in Kiel, is a teacher has one brother. My brother who lives in Kiel has more than one.
  • Quotation marks and full stops. In British English the full stop goes outside unless it belongs to the quotation.

docs.title: How to actually fix this
docs.text:
Reading a list does not change your writing. Two things do.

  1. Keep an error log. One page per term. Three columns: what I wrote, what is correct, why. When the same entry appears twice, that is your personal pattern and it is worth ten minutes.
  2. Do a dedicated checking pass. Not a general reread. One pass looking only for the four or five things on your list. False friends do not feel wrong while you write, which is exactly why they survive a normal reread.

See also: How to read my corrections · How to write a mediation · Useful phrases for writing

docs.title: Quoting and citing: a mini MLA style guide
docs.text:
One consistent way to quote, cite and format titles, used the same way on every page of this handbook and expected the same way in every essay you write.

At a glance

Purpose Quote and cite evidence so it looks the same in every essay, exam or not Structure Short quotes inside the sentence, long quotes set off, titles in italics or quotation marks depending on length Register & voice Formal, consistent punctuation, no decorative quotation marks Length A quote proves a point, it does not replace your point Watch out An unintroduced or unexplained quote earns nothing. "Quote-dumping" is one of the most common, most expensive habits

docs.title: Titles: italics or quotation marks
docs.text:
• Italics for longer, self-contained works: novels, plays, films, collections. Pride and Prejudice, Death of a Salesman.
  • Quotation marks for shorter works or parts of a larger whole: poems, short stories, articles, individual episodes. "The Road Not Taken", "A Modest Proposal".

In handwriting, underline instead of italicizing; the rule is the same.

docs.title: Short quotations
docs.text:
Up to about two lines: keep them inside your own sentence, in quotation marks, grammatically integrated. Do not let a quotation stand as its own sentence with no lead-in.

  • Weak: "The wallpaper is yellow." This shows Gilman uses colour symbolically.
  • Better: Gilman uses colour symbolically, describing the wallpaper as "a smouldering unclean yellow" (l. 47).

docs.title: Long quotations
docs.text: Four lines or more: set off from your own sentence, on its own indented block, without quotation marks. In an exam essay this is rarely worth it, a shorter quote with more analysis around it almost always earns more than a long block with little comment.

docs.title: Citing the source
docs.text:
The whole essay usually refers to one given text, so name it once in full in your introduction (title, author, text type) and then cite briefly after each quote:

  • Poems and plays: line numbers, e.g. (l. 14), or act/scene/line if given, e.g. (II.2.14)
  • Prose extracts: paragraph or page numbers if the task gives them, e.g. (par. 3)
  • No page numbers given: name the quote's position instead, e.g. towards the end of the extract

docs.title: Works Cited: listing your sources
docs.text:
The section above covers a class exam, where you quote the one text you were given. As soon as you use more than one source, in a presentation, a project, or a longer piece of coursework, list every source you actually cite on its own page at the end, headed Works Cited. Each entry is built from the same blocks, in the same order, and you simply skip the blocks that do not apply to your source:

  1. Author.
  2. Title of source.
  3. Title of container,
  4. Other contributors,
  5. Version,
  6. Number,
  7. Publisher,
  8. Publication date,
  9. Location.

Author. Last name first, then first name, ended with a period: Bhabha, Homi K. Two authors: only the first name is inverted, joined by and: Smith, John, and Ana Weber. Leave out titles like Dr. or Prof.

Title of source. Italics for a whole, standalone work (a book, a website, a film). Quotation marks for something that is part of a larger whole (an article, a poem, a single web page, an episode).

Title of container. The larger whole the source sits inside, in italics: the website a page belongs to, the newspaper an article appeared in, the anthology a poem was printed in.

Location. Page numbers for print, or the URL for a web source with http:// removed, ending the entry with a period.

Everything else (a translator, an edition number, a publisher, a date) only gets added when it is actually known and relevant. Most school-level sources need no more than author, title, container and location.

Examples:

  • Book: Bhabha, Homi K. The Location of Culture. Routledge, 1994.
  • Web article: Lundman, Susan. "How to Make Vegetarian Chili." eHow, www.ehow.com/how_10727_make-vegetarian-chili.html.
  • Newspaper article: Bagchi, Alaknanda. "Conflicting Nationalisms." Tulsa Studies in Women's Literature, vol. 15, no. 1, 1996, pp. 41-50.

Formatting the page:

  • Centre the heading Works Cited, do not italicize it or put it in quotation marks. The entries themselves stay flush with the left margin.
  • Sort entries alphabetically by the author's last name. No known author: alphabetize by the title instead.
  • Give the second and any further line of an entry a hanging indent, so the author's name is the only thing that starts at the margin.

docs.title: Changing a quotation
docs.text:
• Omitting words: mark the gap with an ellipsis in square brackets, […]
  • Adding or changing a word to fit your sentence grammatically: put it in square brackets, e.g. the narrator feels "trapped [in her] own home"
  • Never change a quotation silently. If it does not fit your sentence as it stands, quote less or rephrase around it.

docs.title: Punctuation with quotation marks
docs.text:
British convention, used throughout this handbook: the full stop goes outside the closing quotation mark unless it is part of what you are quoting. See False friends and German habits for the fuller rule on commas and relative clauses.

See also: Stylistic devices · How to analyse fictional texts · Useful phrases for writing

docs.title: Operators: what each task word means
docs.text:
The operator tells you exactly what kind of answer is expected. Doing the wrong operation is one of the most expensive mistakes in a class exam: an analysis that only describes loses points even if everything in it is correct.

The exam works with an official list of core operators. The tables below follow that list, in this order: writing, mediation, speaking. Operators outside the list can still appear when their everyday meaning is clear, so a short section at the end covers those too.

At a glance

Purpose Work out what operation a task word actually demands before you start writing or speaking Structure Core operators for writing, then mediation, then speaking, then a few others you may still meet Register & voice Not set by the operator. The text type decides that Length Not set by the operator either. The task and the printed weighting tell you how much to give each part Watch out Doing the wrong operation is the most expensive mistake in a class exam. An analysis that only describes loses marks even when everything in it is true

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
Operator What you have to do analyse, examine Say in detail how the text works and explain it, with evidence from the text. Connect what the text says to its language and form. The task usually names the aspects: Focus on structure and use of language assess, evaluate Reach a well-founded judgement on how valuable, effective or true something is, and back it up with evidence and examples comment (on) Give your own reasoned opinion on something, supported by evidence and examples. You may bring in counterarguments compare Explain what is similar and what differs, with evidence from the text, and tie it to language and form describe Give a detailed account of what a person or thing is like discuss Weigh the arguments for both sides of an issue and reach a reasoned opinion, backed by evidence and examples explain Make clear how or why something is as it is, by drawing on the text and its context outline, summarize, sum up Give a concise account of the main points or ideas, as the task specifies them point out Present the main aspects of something, briefly write (+ text type) Produce a text with the typical features of that type. A second operator in the task says what the text has to do

Two things in this table deserve a second look.

Some operators are one operator with two names. Analyse and examine ask for the same thing, and so do assess and evaluate. The same goes for outline, summarize and sum up. Do not look for a difference in depth between them, there is none.

"Write" almost never comes alone. The task names the text type and then adds a second operator: Write a blog entry in which you assess to what extent …. The first operator sets the format, the second sets the thinking. Both are marked.

docs.title: Mediation
docs.text:
Operator What you have to do outline, present, summarize, sum up Give a concise account of the main points as the task specifies them, and explain culture-related aspects where your addressee needs them write (+ text type) Produce the text type the task names, again explaining culture-related aspects where necessary

The task decides what counts as a main point, not the German text. See How to write a mediation.

docs.title: Speaking
docs.text:
Operator What you have to do agree on, come to an agreement Arrive at one shared opinion or decision, based on arguments analyse, examine Describe the material, explain it and support what you say from it argue Make a case for or against a given view, using suitable evidence assess, evaluate Give a well-founded judgement on the value, quality or significance of something, with arguments comment (on) Give a reasoned opinion, supported by arguments, and consider counterarguments where they help compare Explain what is similar and what differs describe Give a detailed account of what someone or something is like discuss Together with your partner: trade arguments for and against a view and draw a conclusion you can justify explain Make something clear with examples and, where needed, its wider context make suggestions Propose measures or initiatives and say why they should be taken relate (to) Show how two or more texts or ideas oppose, complement or contradict each other

In the speaking exam discuss is a joint task. A good one-sided argument still loses marks if you never let your partner's points change anything. See The speaking exam.

docs.title: Other operators you may meet
docs.text:
These are not on the official core list. A task may still use them when the everyday meaning is obvious, and class tasks use them often.

Operator What you have to do characterize Describe a person's traits and show how the text makes them visible contrast Concentrate on the differences between two things illustrate Make a point clear with examples interpret Explain the deeper meaning of a text or one of its elements in a wider context justify Give solid reasons for a position or decision present Lay out information clearly and in order state Say something clearly and briefly, without discussion

Read the whole task, not just the operator

"Analyse how the author creates suspense" limits the analysis to suspense. The operator sets the operation, the rest of the task sets the focus. Answer exactly that, nothing else.

docs.title: Operators that look alike
docs.text:
These pairs are easy to mix up. Mixing them up is the exact mistake this page exists to prevent.

  • describe vs. analyse: describe stays with what is there, analyse asks how it works and with what effect
  • discuss vs. comment: discuss weighs both sides before it reaches a verdict, comment argues your own opinion and uses counterarguments only to support it
  • outline vs. retell: outline gives the points the task asks about, in your own order and at a higher level than the text. It does not follow the text paragraph by paragraph
  • assess vs. comment: assess judges how far something works or holds true, comment gives your view on an issue
  • interpret vs. analyse: interpret reaches for the deeper meaning in a wider context, analyse stays with evidence and effect in the text itself

docs.title: Paragraph structure and cohesion
docs.text:
Both "topic sentences" and "cohesion" are named directly in the marking scheme, see Exams & grading.

At a glance

Purpose Make a paragraph's job visible in its first sentence, and make paragraphs read as one connected argument, not a pile of separate ones Structure Topic sentence → supporting sentences → (optional) linking sentence into the next paragraph Register & voice Applies to every formal text type in this handbook equally Length A topic sentence is one sentence, not a heading and not a whole paragraph Watch out A topic sentence that only names a topic, without making a claim about it, does not count as one

docs.title: What a topic sentence actually is
docs.text:
A topic sentence does two things at once: it names what the paragraph is about, and it makes a claim about it. Naming the topic alone is not enough.

  • Not a topic sentence: This paragraph is about social media.
  • Topic sentence: Social media has changed how teenagers form friendships, for better and for worse.

Everything else in the paragraph exists to support that one claim, developed with evidence and explanation, not a list of loosely related points.

docs.title: Where it goes
docs.text: Almost always the first sentence of the paragraph. Readers, and markers, use it to predict what is coming; saving it for the middle or the end makes a paragraph harder to follow even when the content itself is good. Creative writing is the exception, where withholding information can be the point, but never in analysis, comment, or discussion paragraphs.

docs.title: Supporting sentences
docs.text: Every sentence after the topic sentence should develop the claim it makes: evidence, an example, an explanation, a consequence. A sentence that does not connect back to the topic sentence belongs in a different paragraph, or nowhere.

docs.title: Linking to the next paragraph
docs.text: A short closing or transition sentence can point forward to the next paragraph's topic, useful in longer essays such as a discussion essay. This is optional, and it is not a conclusion: a conclusion belongs at the end of the whole text, not at the end of every paragraph.

docs.title: Cohesion: connecting the whole text
docs.text:
Cohesion is what the marking scheme means by "connectives, referring back, repeating words and structures, paragraphing" under text organization. It works above the level of a single paragraph.

  • Connectives signal how ideas relate: addition (furthermore, in addition), contrast (however, on the other hand), cause and effect (as a result, consequently), sequence (first, finally). Vary them, repeating also or but every time flattens the argument.
  • Referring back ties a sentence to something already mentioned, using pronouns (it, this, these) or a summarizing noun (this approach, such claims), instead of repeating the full phrase each time.
  • Repeating words and structures on purpose can bind sentences together, a key term echoed across a paragraph, or a deliberately parallel sentence structure. The same connective opening every paragraph is the opposite: it makes the structure feel mechanical rather than connected.
  • Paragraphing is itself a form of cohesion: one paragraph, one idea. A wall of text with no breaks reads as unstructured even when every sentence individually makes sense.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A "topic sentence" that only announces the topic, with no claim: This paragraph will discuss climate change.
  • Starting every paragraph with the same connective
  • A paragraph that drifts away from its own topic sentence halfway through
  • One long paragraph covering the whole argument, with no breaks at all

See also: Exams & grading · How to write a discussion essay · Stylistic devices

docs.title: Poetic form and structure
docs.text:
These are the terms for how a poem is built, not what it says. Use them together with Stylistic devices, which covers imagery, sound and rhetorical patterns, and with How to analyse a poem, which shows how to connect a term like this to an actual argument.

At a glance

Purpose Name the building blocks of a poem's form: stanza, rhyme, rhythm, line Structure Grouped by stanza, rhyme, rhythm and metre, line and syntax, the turn Register & voice Use these terms the same way you use any analytical vocabulary: formal, simple present Length Two or three well-explained terms beat a list of ten Watch out A term is only worth marks once you connect it to meaning. Naming a quatrain earns nothing on its own

docs.title: Stanza
docs.text:
A stanza is a poem's paragraph, a group of lines set off from the next group by a space. Stanzas are named by how many lines they have.

Term Definition Example Stanza A group of lines set off by a space — Couplet Two-line stanza, often rhymed the final two lines of a Shakespearean sonnet Tercet Three-line stanza — Quatrain Four-line stanza, the most common in English poetry most hymn and ballad forms Quintain (cinquain) Five-line stanza each stanza of Frost's "The Road Not Taken" Sestet Six-line stanza, also the second half of a sonnet — Octave Eight-line stanza, also the first half of a sonnet — Sonnet A 14-line poem, usually a single stanza, with a fixed rhyme scheme and a turn Shakespeare's sonnets Free verse No fixed rhyme scheme or metre most 20th- and 21st-century poetry

docs.title: Rhyme
docs.text:
Term What it means Rhyme scheme The pattern of end rhymes, written as letters. The first end sound gets a, the next new end sound gets b, and so on. A sound that returns reuses its letter End rhyme Rhyme at the end of lines, the usual kind Internal rhyme Rhyme within a single line, not just at the end Half rhyme / slant rhyme Sounds are close but not identical, for example worth / north Eye rhyme Words look like they should rhyme, same spelling pattern, but don't sound alike, for example love / move

To find a rhyme scheme, mark the last word of every line and give matching end sounds the same letter as you go. Write it in the margin, one letter per line, then read the pattern down the stanza.

docs.title: Rhythm and metre
docs.text:
You don't need a full scansion of every poem, but knowing the basic units lets you say something precise instead of "the poem has a nice rhythm."

Term Definition Metre A poem's regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables Foot The repeating unit a metre is built from, usually one stressed plus one or more unstressed syllables Iamb / iambic A foot going unstressed–stressed (da-DUM), the most common foot in English Iambic pentameter Five iambic feet per line, ten syllables, the standard line of the English sonnet and of blank verse Iambic tetrameter Four iambic feet per line, eight syllables Stressed / unstressed syllable The syllable that carries more or less emphasis when the line is spoken naturally

A metre that stays regular throughout a poem is worth noticing. A metre that breaks down at one specific point is usually worth more, because the form is doing something at exactly the place where the content changes too.

docs.title: Line and syntax
docs.text: Term Definition Enjambment A sentence or phrase runs past the end of the line, without a pause, into the next line End-stopped line The line ends where the sentence or clause ends, with a natural pause Caesura A pause inside a line, often marked by punctuation such as a comma or dash

docs.title: The turn
docs.text:
Term Definition Volta / turn The point where a poem's argument, mood or perspective shifts. In a sonnet it traditionally sits around line 9, in other poems it can happen anywhere, but it is almost always there somewhere

Finding the turn is usually the fastest way into what a poem is actually doing, see step 5 in How to analyse a poem.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Calling every stanza a quatrain out of habit, without counting the lines
  • Writing out a rhyme scheme without checking each sound against the earlier ones, so the letters no longer match real repeats
  • Forcing a poem into a perfectly regular metre when it is actually irregular, and missing the one line where it isn't, which is often the point
  • Labelling a line break "enjambment" whenever a stanza ends, even where the sentence is already finished

See also: How to analyse a poem · Stylistic devices

docs.title: Register and tone
docs.text:
Register and tone are graded explicitly under text organization ("Appropriateness": register fitting situation and addressee), and naming a tone without evidence is treated the same as spotting a stylistic device without explaining it.

At a glance

Purpose Recognize and set the right register and tone for any text type Structure Register (how formal) first, then tone (the writer's attitude) Register & voice This page is itself neutral, reference language Length A lookup page Watch out Register and tone are not the same thing. A text can be formal and angry, or informal and gentle

docs.title: Register: how formal is the language?
docs.text:
Register is the level of formality, not the writer's mood. Three bands cover almost everything you will read or write.

Feature Formal Neutral Informal Contractions avoided (do not, cannot) occasional frequent (don't, can't) Vocabulary Latinate (obtain, request, commence) everyday (get, ask, start) colloquial (grab, kick off) Sentence length longer, more subordination mixed short, simple Address third person, no direct you unless the addressee is defined some direct address direct, personal (you, we) Passive voice more common occasional rare Modal hedging one might argue, it could be suggested I think, it seems I reckon, kind of Punctuation minimal exclamation marks standard exclamation marks, dashes, ellipses for effect

Which register for which task: analysis and non-fiction essays are formal to neutral, third person, simple present. A comment or discussion is neutral to formal, first person allowed. A speech is neutral to formal but direct, addressing the audience as you/we. An email to a friend inside a mediation or creative task drops into informal. Mediation itself has no fixed register, the addressee and text type set it, see How to write a mediation.

docs.title: Tone: what is the writer's attitude?
docs.text:
Tone is not how formal a text is, it is the writer's attitude to the subject or the reader: serious, ironic, urgent, nostalgic, sympathetic, critical, playful, indignant. A text can shift tone within a single paragraph, name the shift rather than forcing one label onto the whole piece.

How to find it:

  • Word choice. Positively or negatively loaded words reveal attitude before anything else is said. Regime versus government, slashed versus reduced.
  • Stylistic devices. Irony, hyperbole, understatement and rhetorical questions all carry tone, see Stylistic devices.
  • Sentence structure. Short, clipped sentences suggest urgency or tension. Long, flowing sentences suggest reflection or nostalgia.
  • Punctuation. Exclamation marks signal passion or alarm, ellipses suggest hesitation or trailing off, rhetorical questions invite the reader in or challenge them.

A word bank for naming tone:

Category Words Critical critical, scathing, indignant, mocking, ironic, sarcastic Reflective nostalgic, wistful, contemplative, resigned, melancholic Positive hopeful, celebratory, enthusiastic, reassuring, admiring Neutral / informative matter-of-fact, objective, detached, factual Urgent / persuasive urgent, passionate, earnest, alarmed, insistent

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Naming a tone with no evidence. Tone needs the same statement → evidence (quote + line) → effect as any other claim.
  • Using "formal" or "informal" to describe tone. Those words describe register, not attitude.
  • Picking one tone word for a whole text that actually shifts, for example from nostalgic to urgent in the final paragraph.

See also: Stylistic devices · Useful phrases for writing · Operators

docs.title: Spoken text types
docs.text:
Speaking is assessed in the final examination, in class presentations and in every discussion you take part in. This is the quick lookup for everything you say.

At a glance

Purpose Find the conventions of a spoken text type a task asks you to produce Structure One block per text type, always the same five lines Register & voice Every block names both, because markers check both Length Where a task gives no word count, use the figures here as a default Watch out The task always beats this page. If it names a register or an addressee, that wins

The five lines below mean the same thing on every page of this handbook:

  • Purpose — what the text is supposed to do to its reader or listener
  • Structure — the skeleton a marker expects to find
  • Register & voice — formality, grammatical person, tense
  • Length — a workable default when the task is silent
  • Watch out — the mistake that costs most marks in this particular type

docs.title: Presentation
docs.text: Purpose Make an audience understand and remember something they did not know Structure Greeting → attention-grabbing introduction → main part → conclusion → invitation to questions Register & voice Neutral to formal. First person, addressing the audience directly. Simple present Length As set. Roughly 130 words per minute of speech Watch out Do not read full sentences from your notes. Explain technical terms, avoid words your classmates will not know, use visuals to support rather than repeat you. In a group presentation every member must carry a real share

docs.title: Speech
docs.text: Purpose Move an audience to think, feel or do something Structure Introduction → main part → conclusion, all serving one message Register & voice Neutral to formal. First person, direct address. Simple present Length As set. Roughly 130 words per minute Watch out State your intention clearly. Pauses, emphasis and eye contact are part of the performance and are marked. Full page: How to write a speech

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text: Purpose Work through an issue with others and let positions meet Structure Open with your position → argue with examples → respond to others → move towards a shared conclusion Register & voice Neutral to formal. First person. Simple present Length As set Watch out Participate without dominating. Listen, refer back to what others said, take turns. This is the same skill the paired speaking exam tests: The speaking exam

docs.title: Dialogue
docs.text: Purpose Play out an exchange between two people convincingly Structure Opening → exchange with genuine turn-taking → closing Register & voice Set by the roles. First person in role. Tense as the situation requires Length As set Watch out Stay in role, react to what your partner actually said, and keep it polite even when the roles disagree

docs.title: Interview
docs.text: Purpose Draw information or a position out of someone for an audience Structure Introduction of guest and topic → questions grouped sensibly → closing thanks Register & voice Neutral to formal. First and second person. Simple present, past for what happened Length As set Watch out Open questions produce answers, closed questions produce nothing. Follow up on what the guest says instead of working through a fixed list

docs.title: Podcast
docs.text: Purpose Hold a listener who cannot see you and cannot skim Structure Title and topic → introduction that hooks → main part → conclusion Register & voice Informal to neutral, matched to the audience. Neutral or first person. Simple present Length As set Watch out Signpost far more than you would in writing. Imagery, exaggeration and rhetorical questions carry a listener; music, quotations or a short interview clip can support a point

docs.title: Role play
docs.text: Purpose Act out a situation from a defined perspective Structure As the scenario requires Register & voice Determined by your role, not by your own habits Length As set Watch out Everything you say should be something your character would say. Breaking role to comment on it costs marks

docs.title: The pattern behind all of them
docs.text:
Spoken types are judged on the same five questions as written ones, with one addition that never appears in writing: delivery. Volume, pace, eye contact, gesture and the use of pauses are marked, not decoration.

  • What is this supposed to do to the people listening?
  • What skeleton will they expect?
  • What register, what person, what tense?
  • How long, and does the task say?
  • What would make this fail its type?
  • Can I be heard, followed and looked at while I do it?

See also: How to give a presentation · Discussions and debates · The speaking exam

docs.title: Stylistic devices
docs.text:
For every device you name in an analysis: quote it, give the line, explain the effect in context. The "typical effect" column is a starting point, not a ready-made answer.

At a glance

Purpose Name a device correctly and, more importantly, say what it does Structure Grouped by what the device works on: imagery, sound, structure, argument Register & voice Analysis is formal, neutral perspective, simple present Length Two or three well-explained devices beat a list of ten Watch out Statement → evidence (quote + line) → effect. docs.text: Device Definition Example Typical effect Anaphora Repetition at the start of successive sentences or lines We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds … (Churchill) Builds rhythm and intensity; hammers a point home Repetition Repeating a word or phrase Never, never, never give up Emphasis; makes the key idea stick Parallelism Same grammatical structure in successive parts Easy come, easy go Balance and clarity; invites comparison Rule of three Three parallel elements blood, sweat and tears Feels complete and forceful; highly memorable Enumeration Listing of items He packed shirts, books, hopes and doubts Creates abundance or urgency; can build to a climax Climax Arrangement from weakest to strongest He came, he saw, he conquered Rising intensity toward the key point Anticlimax Sudden drop from important to trivial He lost his empire, his army and his umbrella Deflates; often humorous or satirical Antithesis Opposed ideas in parallel form One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind (Armstrong) Sharpens contrast; memorable phrasing Inversion Unusual word order Never have I seen such courage Emphasizes the fronted element; formal or dramatic tone Chiasmus Second phrase mirrors the first Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country (Kennedy) Elegant reversal; makes the idea feel conclusive

docs.title: Words you will hear
docs.text:
This handbook is written in English throughout. School, however, runs in German, and on an examination day nobody will hand you a "fair copy" sheet. This is the one page where both languages sit side by side, so that you can match what you read here to what you are told in the corridor.

At a glance

Purpose Match the English terms used in this handbook to the official German ones you will actually hear Structure Grouped by where you meet the word: the course, assessment, the examination day Register & voice Official terminology. None of it belongs in an English text you write Length One page. It is a lookup, not a reading task Watch out Never use the German terms in your own English writing. docs.title: Written text types
docs.text:
Every open task names a text type, and the text type decides your structure, your register and your perspective before you write a single sentence. This is the quick lookup for everything you write.

At a glance

Purpose Find the conventions of a written text type a task asks you to produce Structure One block per text type, always the same five lines Register & voice Every block names both, because markers check both Length Where a task gives no word count, use the figures here as a default Watch out The task always beats this page. If it names a register or an addressee, that wins

The five lines below mean the same thing on every page of this handbook:

  • Purpose — what the text is supposed to do to its reader or listener
  • Structure — the skeleton a marker expects to find
  • Register & voice — formality, grammatical person, tense
  • Length — a workable default when the task is silent
  • Watch out — the mistake that costs most marks in this particular type

docs.title: Argumentative text, comment, essay
docs.text: Purpose Convince a reader of a position, having shown that you know the other side exists Structure Introductory sentence → arguments with examples → conclusion. Order the arguments deliberately: antithetical, progressive, or problem to solution Register & voice Neutral to formal. Neutral or first person. Simple present Length 200 to 350 words Watch out An argument without an example is an assertion. Paragraphs need topic sentences, and stylistic devices should work on the reader, not decorate the page

docs.title: Article
docs.text: Purpose Inform a defined readership about a subject and hold their attention while doing it Structure Attention-grabbing headline → introduction → main part in paragraphs → conclusion Register & voice Depends on the publication named in the task: informal for a school magazine, formal for a broadsheet. Neutral or first person. Present tense for the state of things, past for events Length 250 to 400 words Watch out Write the headline last and make it specific. Reported speech where you refer to what others said

docs.title: Blog post
docs.text: Purpose Share a personal take on a topic and invite a response Structure Short, pointed headline → lead paragraph that explains why to read on → short paragraphs, ideally with subheadings → conclusion that answers the headline and may call for action → date Register & voice Informal to neutral, matched to the target group. First person. Simple present Length 250 to 350 words Watch out Put the most interesting element in the first paragraph, not the last. A blog post that reads like an essay has missed the type

docs.title: Diary entry
docs.text: Purpose Record a moment and what it did to the writer, from inside their head Structure Date → the event → thoughts, worries and feelings about it → an open ending or a resolution Register & voice Neutral to informal. First person. Past tense for the events, present for the reflection Length 150 to 250 words Watch out Only what the character could plausibly know. No narrator knowledge, no information from later in the text. Short, sometimes elliptical sentences, exclamations and questions are right here

docs.title: Email or letter, formal
docs.text: Purpose Achieve something specific from an institution or a stranger: information, a decision, a correction Structure (Addresses) → date → subject line or reference → salutation → short opening naming your reason for writing → main part → closing request or question → complimentary close → full name Register & voice Formal throughout. First person. Present tense, future for what you expect Length 200 to 300 words Watch out Dear Sir or Madam pairs with Yours faithfully, Dear Mr/Ms X with Yours sincerely. No contractions, no slang. Accuracy is judged more strictly here than anywhere else

docs.title: Email or letter, informal
docs.text: Purpose Keep in touch with someone you know and tell them something that matters to you Structure Salutation → main part → closing → first name Register & voice Neutral to informal. First person. Contractions and phrasal verbs are welcome Length 150 to 250 words Watch out Informal is not careless. Feelings and exclamations belong here, spelling mistakes do not

docs.title: Letter to the editor
docs.text: Purpose React publicly to a published article and put your own position against it Structure Salutation → name the article and summarize the position you are answering → discuss it → state your own view → closing remarks → complimentary close → full name Register & voice Neutral to formal. First person. Simple present Length 200 to 300 words Watch out The reference to the original article belongs in the first two sentences. Readers of the paper have not necessarily read it

docs.title: Letter of application, personal statement
docs.text: Purpose Get an interview or a place by matching your qualities to a specific position Structure Your address and theirs → date → subject line → salutation → the post and where you saw it → why you are interested → the skills that make you suitable, with evidence → what you know about the organization → request for an interview → mention of enclosures → close → full name Register & voice Neutral to formal. First person. Present perfect for what you have done, present for what you can do Length One page, no more Watch out Claims without evidence are worthless. Every skill you name should point to something you have actually done

docs.title: Outline
docs.text: Purpose Set out the relevant information from a text in a compact, ordered form Structure Introductory sentence with text type, title, author, source, date and topic → the key information in a logical order Register & voice Neutral. Neutral point of view. Simple present, reported speech where needed Length Shorter than a summary, driven by what the task calls relevant Watch out Outline, summarize and sum up are one operator: a concise account of the main points as the task specifies. Select by the task and abstract, do not retell. No opinion

docs.title: Report
docs.text: Purpose Give an accurate, impersonal account of an event to someone who was not there Structure Summarizing opening sentence → the events in chronological order → outcome Register & voice Neutral to formal. Neutral perspective. Past tenses. Passive and reported speech where they fit Length 200 to 300 words Watch out No thoughts, no feelings, no opinions. If the event is fictional, invent the missing names, places and dates rather than leaving gaps

docs.title: Review
docs.text: Purpose Help a reader decide whether a book, film or play is worth their time Structure Introduction with title, author or director, year and genre → outline of the plot without the ending → discussion of beginning, plot development, characters, setting → recommendation Register & voice Neutral to informal, depending on the publication. First person for the judgement. Simple present Length 250 to 350 words Watch out Never give away the ending. A recommendation without reasons is not a review, it is a rating

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Purpose Let a reader who does not know the text understand what it says Structure Introductory sentence with text type, title, author, source, date and topic → key statements in a logical order → optional closing sentence Register & voice Neutral to formal. Neutral point of view. Simple present. Reported speech where needed Length As set by the task. Class rule of thumb: about one third of the original Watch out Own words throughout. Class rule of thumb: no more than four consecutive words from the source. No examples, no quotations, no opinion. Full page: How to write an outline or summary

docs.title: Mediation
docs.text: Purpose Give an English-speaking addressee exactly the content from a German source that they need for a stated purpose Structure The structure of the text type the task demands, not the structure of the source Register & voice Set by addressee and text type. Name the source early. Perspective as the task defines it Length About one quarter of the source. In the final examination the source is at most 650 words Watch out Relevance is decided by the task, not by the text. No word-for-word translation, no German sentence patterns, no additions of your own. Full page: How to write a mediation

docs.title: The pattern behind all of them
docs.text:
Every one of these blocks answers the same five questions, and every marking scheme asks them in the same order. When a task names a text type you have never practised, work through the five lines yourself:

  • What is this text supposed to do to its reader?
  • What skeleton does a reader of this type expect?
  • What register, what person, what tense?
  • How long, and does the task say?
  • What is the one thing that would make this text fail its type?

Answer those and you have a plan, whatever the type.

See also: Useful phrases for writing · Operators · Exams & grading

See also: Spoken text types · Useful phrases for writing · Operators

docs.title: Discussions and debates
docs.text:
Two different formats with two different goals. A discussion looks for the best answer together. A debate assigns you a side and asks you to win. Both are marked on how you deal with other people, not only on what you know.

At a glance

Purpose Discussion: work out an issue together. Debate: argue an assigned side under fixed rules Structure Discussion: position → argument → response → shared conclusion. Debate: opening speeches → rebuttals → closing speeches Register & voice Neutral to formal. First person. Simple present. Polite even when you disagree sharply Length As set. In a debate the speaking times are part of the rules Watch out Participate without dominating. Listening and responding are marked as heavily as speaking

Operators that show up in this task type:

Operator Example task discuss Discuss in pairs whether social media should be regulated more strictly. argue Argue for or against a ban on mobile phones in lessons. justify Justify your position after listening to your partner's arguments. assess Assess the strongest argument you heard from the other side.

See Operators for what each of these actually asks for.

docs.title: Discussion or debate?
docs.text: Discussion Debate Goal Understand the issue better Convince the audience or the judges Your position Your own Assigned, often the one you disagree with Rules Loose, turn-taking by courtesy Fixed speaking order and times Success looks like The group has moved somewhere Your side stood up to attack The real skill Building on other people Anticipating the counterargument

docs.title: How a discussion works
docs.text:
1. Open with a position, not a hedge. "It depends" is where you finish, not where you start.
  2. Give one argument with one piece of evidence. Then stop and let someone answer.
  3. Listen for what is actually said, not for the gap where you can insert your next point.
  4. Take up what others said by name. "Building on what Jonas said about …" costs you two seconds and earns interaction marks.
  5. Disagree with the argument, never with the person.
  6. Ask when you do not follow. A clarifying question is a contribution, not an admission of weakness.
  7. Move towards a conclusion. In the last minutes, name where the group agrees and where it does not.

docs.title: How a debate works
docs.text:
A common classroom format, adapt to whatever rules you are given:

Stage Who Time Opening statement Proposition 2 min Opening statement Opposition 2 min Free debate Both sides alternating 6 min Closing statement Opposition 1 min Closing statement Proposition 1 min

Three things decide a debate more often than knowledge does:

  • Definitions. Whoever defines the terms of the motion has already shaped the ground. Do it in the first thirty seconds.
  • Rebuttal. A point left unanswered counts as conceded. Answer the strongest argument against you, not the weakest.
  • The closing. Do not summarize everything. Name the one clash your side won.

docs.title: Buying yourself a second
docs.text:
Everyone needs thinking time. In a foreign language you need slightly more, and silence is more expensive than a filler. Use a full sentence rather than "ehm":

  • That is a difficult one. Let me think for a moment.
  • I want to get this right, so let me put it another way.
  • Two things come to mind. First, …

docs.title: Checklist for a discussion or debate
docs.text:
• Did I state a clear position rather than hedging?
  • Did every argument come with evidence or an example?
  • Did I refer to at least two other speakers by what they said?
  • Did I disagree with an argument without attacking a person?
  • Did I ask at least one genuine question?
  • Did I leave space for people who had not spoken?
  • In a debate: did I answer the strongest point against my side?
  • In a debate: does my closing name the clash rather than summarize everything?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Waiting for a gap to deliver a prepared speech instead of responding to what is happening
  • Agreeing with everything, which produces a short flat conversation and costs marks in content and interaction alike
  • Dominating. Talking for eight of ten minutes loses the same category as saying nothing
  • Attacking the person: "That is a stupid argument" instead of "That argument does not work here, because …"
  • Leaving the strongest counterargument unanswered and hoping nobody noticed
  • Reading from notes. Notes are keywords, a conversation cannot be scripted

See also: Socratic seminar · How to give a presentation · The speaking exam

docs.title: How to give a presentation
docs.text:
At a glance

Purpose Make an audience understand and remember something they did not know Structure Greeting → hook → outline of your points → main part → conclusion → questions Register & voice Neutral to formal. First person, addressing the audience directly. Simple present Length As set. Roughly 130 words per minute, so ten minutes is about 1300 words spoken Watch out Never read full sentences from your notes. Keywords only, eyes up

Operators that show up in this task type:

Operator Example task present Present the results of your survey to the class. illustrate Illustrate your point with examples from your research.

present is the operator this task type is named after, it is almost always the one used. See Operators.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Fix your one message first. Before you research anything, write down in one sentence what the audience should know or think afterwards. Everything that does not serve that sentence gets cut later, so decide now.
  2. Research from more than one source. Compare what they say. Where they disagree, you have found something worth presenting.
  3. Note where everything came from. You will need it for your source slide, and taking someone else's work without saying so is not a small thing.
  4. Choose three points, no more. An audience listening in a foreign language will hold on to three things. Five points means they remember none of them.
  5. Build the skeleton. Hook, outline, three points with evidence, conclusion that answers the hook.
  6. Write the hook last but rehearse it first. A question, a surprising figure, a thirty-second story. Never "Today I am going to talk about …".
  7. Make the visuals carry pictures, not text. A slide is a poster behind you, not a script in front of you. If your audience is reading, they are not listening.
  8. Reduce your notes to keywords. One index card, six keywords. If you can present from that, you know your material.
  9. Rehearse out loud, timed, standing up. Silent rehearsal at your desk tells you nothing about pace or breathing.
  10. Prepare for questions. Two or three you expect, and a way of saying you do not know that does not collapse the whole talk.

docs.title: Structure in detail
docs.text: Stage What happens Roughly Greeting Name yourself and your topic 15 seconds Hook Question, figure, image or short story 30 seconds Outline Tell them your three points in advance 20 seconds Main part Point, evidence, why it matters. Three times 70 % of your time Conclusion Return to the hook, state the one message 45 seconds Questions Invite them, answer briefly as available

docs.title: Useful phrases
docs.text:
Purpose Phrases Opening
  • Good morning everyone. My name is … and today I would like to talk about …
  • Let me start with a number that surprised me: …
  • Have you ever wondered why … ?
Giving an outline
  • I have divided my talk into three parts.
  • First I will …, then I will …, and finally I will …
  • Feel free to interrupt me if anything is unclear.
Moving between points
  • That brings me to my second point.
  • Having looked at …, let us turn to …
  • So much for … . Now, …
Referring to a visual
  • As you can see on this slide, …
  • This graph shows …
  • Let me draw your attention to the figure on the right.
  • The numbers speak for themselves: …
Emphasizing
  • What matters most here is …
  • If you take away one thing today, let it be this: …
  • And this is the surprising part: …
Explaining a term
  • By … I mean …
  • For those who have not come across the term, …
  • Put simply, …
Involving the audience
  • Put yourself in their position for a moment.
  • How many of you have ever … ?
  • We all know the feeling.
Concluding
  • To sum up, …
  • Let me come back to the question I started with.
  • Thank you for listening. I am happy to take your questions.
Handling questions
  • That is a good question. As far as I know, …
  • I am not sure about that, but what I can say is …
  • Could you say a little more about what you mean?

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Delivery is marked, not decoration. The examination criteria for speaking are content, interaction and language, and delivery is how the first two reach anyone at all.

  • Volume and pace. Slower than feels natural. Nerves speed everyone up.
  • Eye contact. Pick three people in different parts of the room and rotate.
  • Pauses. After a key sentence, and before you move to a new point. Silence gives the audience a moment to catch up.
  • Your voice. Emphasis on the word that carries the meaning, not on every third word.
  • Hands. Somewhere visible and still, or gesturing on purpose. Not in your pockets and not on your phone.
  • Stand where they can see you, not in front of the projection.

docs.title: In a group presentation
docs.text: Everyone must carry a real share. A person who introduces the group and then falls silent has not presented. Divide by content, not by slide count, and hand over explicitly: "Lisa will now take you through the second part."

docs.title: Checklist for a presentation
docs.text:
• Can I say my one message in a single sentence?
  • Three points, not five?
  • Does the hook survive being said out loud?
  • Do my slides show images and figures rather than sentences?
  • Are my notes keywords, not full sentences?
  • Have I timed a full run-through, standing and out loud?
  • Have I explained every technical term I use?
  • Are my sources named on a final slide?
  • Do I know what to say if I do not know an answer?
  • In a group: does every member have a real share?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading the slides aloud. The audience can read faster than you can speak, and they will
  • Five or six points, all of them thin, instead of three developed ones
  • A hook that is really an announcement: "Today I am going to talk about …"
  • Technical terms left unexplained because they were clear in the source
  • Speaking to the screen instead of to the room
  • Running over time, which almost always means the conclusion gets rushed and the one message never lands

See also: Discussions and debates · Spoken text types · The speaking exam

docs.title: Socratic seminar
docs.text:
A seminar is not a debate and not a normal class discussion. Nobody wins it. The group works its way into a text together, and the questions matter more than the answers.

At a glance

Purpose Understand the ideas, issues and values in a text by talking through them as a group Structure Preparation with the text → opening question → the group carries the conversation → closing reflection Register & voice Neutral to formal. First person. Tentative rather than assertive Length Usually one lesson. Inner circle around 20 to 30 minutes Watch out You are not here to win. Asserting opinions or proving an argument is the one thing a seminar is not for

Operators that show up in this task type:

Operator Example task interpret Interpret what the text suggests about the narrator's state of mind. discuss Discuss how your readings of the text differ within the group. relate Relate this text to the ideas raised in the text discussed last week.

See Operators for what each of these actually asks for.

docs.title: What makes it different
docs.text:
Socratic seminar Debate Normal discussion Goal Understand the text together Convince Exchange views Your job Ask, listen, connect Argue a side State your view Who leads The group The rules Usually the teacher Evidence Always from the text Anything persuasive Often personal experience A good moment Someone changes their mind Someone is cornered Someone makes a point

The teacher is not the one asking the questions. That takes some getting used to, and the first two minutes are always the hardest. Somebody has to start, and the silence before that is normal.

docs.title: Preparing the text
docs.text:
Preparation is the whole seminar. An unprepared circle runs out after four minutes.

  1. Read carefully and take your time. Once for the sense, once with a pencil.
  2. Note what strikes you. Significant points, images that recur, sentences you had to read twice.
  3. Read critically. What is the purpose of this text? What are its central themes? What is it not saying?
  4. Identify the key ideas, arguments and perspectives it puts forward.
  5. Write questions. Open, genuinely open. Three is a good target, and see the next section.
  6. Collect evidence. For every idea you want to raise, mark the line you would point to.
  7. Consider the other reading. What would someone who disagrees with you say, and where in the text would they look?

docs.title: What makes a good seminar question
docs.text:
A question you already know the answer to is not a question, it is a quiz item.

Weak Better Who is the narrator? What does the narrator want us not to notice? Is the lion a good character? What does the text seem to think we owe to someone who once had power over us? Does the tree love the boy? Where does giving stop being generous in this text? What happens at the end? Why does the text end here rather than one page later?

Three types worth having in your notes:

  • Opening question. Broad, no single answer, points back to the text. Good for the first five minutes.
  • Core question. Goes at the heart of the text's problem. This is the one you hope the group spends most of its time on.
  • Closing question. Connects the text to something beyond it, without leaving it behind.

docs.title: Language for the circle
docs.text:
Purpose Phrases Asking for clarification
  • Can you please elaborate on that?
  • I am not sure I understand. Can you clarify?
  • Can you give me an example of what you mean?
  • Can you explain that in a different way?
  • I am sorry, I do not quite follow.
Checking understanding
  • What are you assuming when you say … ?
  • If I understand correctly, … . Is that right?
  • How does this relate to what we have been discussing?
  • I want to make sure I understood you correctly. Did you mean … ?
Questioning and evaluating
  • Can you explain why this is important?
  • Can you provide some evidence for that?
  • How did you come to that conclusion?
  • Can you explain your reasoning?
  • What are your overall impressions of this passage?
Disagreeing
  • I am afraid I do not agree with that statement.
  • I see things differently.
  • I understand your point of view, but I disagree, because …
  • I disagree with your conclusion, because …
Agreeing and adding
  • I could not agree more.
  • I support that.
  • I am on the same page.
  • I agree and would like to add …
  • I completely agree and I would also like to point out …
Anchoring in the text
  • If we look at line 12, …
  • The text actually says …, which is not quite the same thing.
  • There is a word here that I keep coming back to: …
Opening space
  • We have not heard from everyone yet.
  • Does anyone read that differently?
  • Could we stay with this passage a little longer?
Changing your mind
  • I came in thinking …, and I am no longer sure.
  • That reading is better than mine, because …

Changing your mind out loud is the most valuable thing that can happen in a seminar. It is not a defeat, and it is worth saying when it happens.

docs.title: If you are in the outer circle
docs.text:
Many seminars run with an inner circle talking and an outer circle observing. The outer circle is not a break.

  • Follow one speaker and note how often they build on someone else
  • Note where the conversation lost the text and started running on opinion
  • Note the question that produced the most movement
  • Be ready to feed that back afterwards

docs.title: Checklist for a Socratic seminar
docs.text:
• Have I read the text at least twice, with a pencil?
  • Do I have three open questions written down?
  • For each idea I want to raise, do I know the line I would point to?
  • Have I thought about how someone might read this differently?
  • Do I know six phrases for clarifying and disagreeing?
  • Am I ready to speak in the first five minutes?
  • Am I ready to stop talking and let a silence sit?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Arriving unprepared. It is visible within two minutes and it costs the whole group
  • Treating it as a debate and trying to win
  • Opinion without text. "I just feel that …" with nothing to point at
  • Speaking to the teacher instead of to the circle
  • Waiting for the perfect sentence. An imperfect contribution in English beats a perfect one you never said
  • Filling every silence. A pause usually means people are thinking

See also: Discussions and debates · Spoken text types · How to analyse fictional texts

docs.title: How to write a characterization
docs.text:
A characterization is an analysis with a person at the centre. Everything you claim about a character has to come from the text, and the interesting part is almost never what a character says about themselves.

At a glance

Purpose Show what a character is like and how the text makes us see them that way Structure Introduction → outward facts → behaviour and relationships → inner life → function in the text Register & voice Formal, neutral perspective, simple present Length As set by the task Watch out Statement → evidence (quote + line) → effect. A list of adjectives is not a characterization

Operators for this task type: characters are usually set through analyse, not through the word "characterize" itself, keep that in mind.

Operator Example task analyse — most common, remember this one Analyse Hector's character and the way Alan Bennett creates it. (Abitur 2009) compare Compare Hector's and Irwin's attitudes towards education. (Abitur 2009, same paper) characterize Not on the official core list, but it names this page and may turn up. Rarely the literal task word

See Operators.

docs.title: Direct and indirect characterization
docs.text:
This distinction carries most of the marks.

Where it comes from How much it is worth Direct The narrator or another character tells us what someone is like Easy to find, easy to be misled by Indirect What the character does, says, thinks, how others react to them, how they are described Where the real analysis happens

Direct statements are evidence about the speaker as much as about the person described. If a narrator calls someone selfish, the first question is whether the narrator is reliable.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Read with one character in mind. Second reading, pencil, only their scenes.
  2. Collect in four columns: what they say, what they do, what they think, how others react to them.
  3. Look for the gap. Between what a character says and what they do, between how they see themselves and how others see them. That gap is usually the point of the character.
  4. Group your findings into traits. Three or four well-evidenced traits beat eight assertions.
  5. Order them. Outward and factual first, inner life last, because the inner life is what you had to work for.
  6. Write each paragraph as claim, evidence, effect. Trait, quotation with line reference, what it tells us and how the text achieves it.
  7. Ask what the character is for. Do they drive the plot, embody a theme, act as a foil to someone else? This is the paragraph that lifts a characterization out of the middle band.
  8. Check for development. Is the character at the end the same as at the beginning? If not, name the turning point.

docs.title: Structure in detail
docs.text: Section What goes in it Introduction Title, author, year, text type, and who this character is in one sentence Outward facts Age, background, occupation, appearance, social position, only where the text gives them Behaviour and relationships How they act, how they treat others, how others react to them Language How they speak: register, sentence length, what they avoid saying Inner life Motives, fears, values, contradictions Development Do they change? Where, and what triggers it? Function What the character does for the text: theme, foil, contrast, plot

docs.title: Useful phrases
docs.text:
Purpose Phrases Introducing the character
  • … is the first-person narrator of …
  • The reader first meets … in the opening paragraph, where …
  • … is introduced as a minor figure and turns out to be central to …
Direct characterization
  • The narrator describes her as "…" (l. 12).
  • According to …, he is "…" (l. 30), although the text later undercuts this.
Indirect characterization
  • His behaviour towards … reveals that …
  • The way she addresses her mother suggests …
  • That he says nothing at this point is more telling than any answer.
  • Other characters react to him with …, which indicates …
Language as evidence
  • Her short, clipped sentences convey …
  • He uses the vocabulary of business even when talking about his family, which …
  • The repeated "…" (ll. 5, 19) marks him as …
Naming a contradiction
  • What he says and what he does pull in different directions: …
  • She presents herself as …, yet the text shows her …
Development
  • Up to this point, … . After the encounter with …, however, …
  • The turning point comes in l. 41, when …
  • By the end of the extract, she has moved from … to …
Function
  • … serves as a foil to …, throwing his … into relief.
  • Through …, the text explores the question of …
  • The character embodies the conflict between … and …
Concluding
  • Taken together, these details present a character who …
  • The text builds … less through description than through …

docs.title: Checklist for a characterization
docs.text:
• Does every trait I name have a quotation with a line reference?
  • Have I used indirect evidence, not only what the narrator states?
  • Have I checked whether the direct statements come from a reliable source?
  • Have I found and named at least one contradiction or gap?
  • Have I used the character's own language as evidence?
  • Have I said what the character is for in this text?
  • Have I checked whether the character develops, and named the turning point?
  • Simple present throughout?
  • No more than four consecutive words taken from the source?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A list of adjectives with no evidence: "She is brave, intelligent and stubborn"
  • Retelling the plot in the order it happens, with the character mentioned along the way
  • Taking the narrator at their word without asking whether they are reliable
  • Judging the character morally instead of analysing them
  • Missing the function paragraph, which is where the analysis stops being a description
  • Slipping into the past tense because the story is told in the past tense

See also: How to analyse fictional texts · Stylistic devices · Written text types

docs.title: How to write a comment
docs.text:
At a glance

Purpose State your opinion on an issue and make a reader accept it Structure Statement of opinion → arguments with evidence → conclusion Register & voice Neutral to formal, first person, simple present Length As set by the task, typically 200 to 300 words Watch out A comment is not a discussion. You argue your side. Sitting on the fence fails the task

Operators for this task type:

Operator Example task comment (on) — the single most common operator on the whole exam, remember this one Comment on this proverb referring to different views presented in the text. (Abitur 2008) evaluate Evaluate Garth Brooks' vision of an ideal society and compare it to your personal opinion on the topic. (Abitur 2008) justify Not on the official core list, worth knowing even though it rarely turns up as the literal task word

See Operators.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Collect ideas. A quick mind map of pro and contra points helps you see which side you can argue more convincingly, even though you will mainly present one side.
  2. Take a position. Decide before you write. A comment that sits on the fence fails its purpose.
  3. Write your introductory statement. State the issue and your opinion on it, with a clear link to the text or question you were given.
  4. Build the argumentation. Two to four arguments, each in its own paragraph: claim → reason → example or evidence. Order them from weakest to strongest, so your best point comes last.
  5. Deal with one counterargument. Concede it briefly, then refute it ("Admittedly, … However, …"). This makes your position stronger, not weaker.
  6. Conclude. Return to your opinion, sharpened by the arguments. Do not introduce new points here.

docs.title: Useful phrases
docs.text:
Purpose Phrases Stating your opinion
  • In my opinion, …
  • I am convinced that …
  • It seems clear to me that …
  • I would argue that …
Giving reasons
  • The main reason is …
  • This is because …
  • … , which shows that …
  • The evidence for this is …
Giving examples
  • For instance, …
  • A case in point is …
  • This can be seen in …
  • Take … as an example.
Conceding and refuting
  • Admittedly, … However, …
  • It is true that …, but …
  • Critics may argue that …, yet …
  • There is something in this view, and still …
Concluding
  • To conclude, …
  • All things considered, …
  • For these reasons, I believe that …

docs.title: Checklist for a comment
docs.text:
• Clear position stated in the first paragraph?
  • Each argument in its own paragraph with reason and example?
  • Arguments ordered weakest to strongest?
  • One counterargument addressed and refuted?
  • Conclusion matches the opinion you started with?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Retelling the text instead of arguing about the issue
  • Listing opinions without reasons or examples
  • Switching sides in the middle of the text
  • A conclusion that suddenly introduces a brand-new argument

docs.title: How to write a creative text
docs.text:
In the examination this is one of the two options in the final sub-task. The other is a personal response. Both are marked with the same rigour, and creative does not mean free: you are writing inside a text somebody else made.

At a glance

Purpose Extend, continue or re-angle a given text without contradicting it Structure The structure of the form you were asked for: diary entry, letter, monologue, continuation Register & voice The character's, not yours. Tense follows the form Length As set by the task, typically 200 to 300 words Watch out Nothing may contradict the source. Invention is welcome, contradiction is a content error

Operators for this task type: creative briefs skip the analytical operators, the task simply says write, and the brief itself sets what the text has to do.

Instruction Example task write (the only operator used) — remember this one Write a love letter to the United Kingdom expressing appreciation of two of the following aspects: history, politics, science, culture. (Abitur 2017) continue (not a formal operator, but common in class) Continue the story from the point where the extract breaks off.

See Operators for how the formal operators work in the other task types.

docs.title: The rule that decides everything
docs.text:
A creative task is marked on how well your text fits the one you were given. The marking criteria ask for convincing ideas realized in the right text type, with a clear sense of situation and addressee, and for reference back to the material.

That means two things at once:

  • You may invent. Names, weather, a memory, a room, a smell, what happened the next morning.
  • You may not contradict. Not the events, not the relationships, not what a character can plausibly know at that point in the story.

Every sentence you write should survive the question: could this be true in the world of the original text?

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Read the task twice and underline three things: the form, the character or voice, and the moment in the text you are writing from.
  2. Go back to the source and mine it. What does this character notice? What words do they use? What do they avoid saying? Mark five details you can reuse.
  3. Fix the moment. Exactly when does your text happen? Before the extract, during it, an hour after, ten years later? Everything else follows from that.
  4. Fix what the character knows at that moment. Write it down. This is the single most common place marks are lost.
  5. Plan three beats. Even 250 words need a shape: a situation, a turn, a landing.
  6. Write in their voice, not yours. Educated adult narrator and frightened fourteen-year-old do not share a vocabulary.
  7. Anchor it in the source at least twice. Not with quotations, with details a reader of the original will recognize.
  8. Revise for range. Creative writing is still marked on lexis and grammar. Imagery is not an excuse for loose sentences.

docs.title: The four forms you are most likely to get
Diary entry
docs.text: Voice First person, past for the events, present for reflection Structure Date → what happened → what it did to me → an open ending or a resolution Typical move Address the diary directly, use short and sometimes unfinished sentences Watch out Only what the writer could know. No narrator knowledge

docs.title: Interior monologue
docs.text: Voice First person, present tense, unfiltered Structure No structure on the surface, a clear one underneath: a thought that circles and shifts Typical move Associative jumps, repetitions, questions with no answer, sentence fragments Watch out It must still be readable. Stream of consciousness is not an excuse for chaos

docs.title: Letter to a character
docs.text: Voice First person, addressed to a named person you know something about Structure Salutation → why I am writing → what I want to say → what I want from you → close Typical move Refer to a shared moment from the text so the reader knows you were there Watch out Register follows the relationship. A letter to a parent and to a stranger are not the same text

docs.title: Continuation of a story
docs.text: Voice The same narrative perspective as the original, unless the task says otherwise Structure Pick up mid-motion, develop, land somewhere Typical move Keep the original's tense, rhythm and level of detail Watch out Do not resolve everything. A continuation that ties up every thread reads as a summary

docs.title: Useful phrases
docs.text:
Purpose Phrases Opening a diary entry
  • I still do not know what to make of today.
  • It is late, and I cannot stop thinking about …
  • Something happened this afternoon that I need to write down.
Interior monologue
  • Why did I say that. Why did I say that.
  • Keep walking. Do not look back.
  • Later. I will think about it later.
Opening a letter
  • You will be surprised to hear from me.
  • I have started this letter four times.
  • There is something I should have said to you that evening.
Referring back to the source
  • Ever since that afternoon at …
  • You said something then that I have never forgotten.
  • It was the same room, only quieter.
Showing feeling without naming it
  • My hands would not keep still.
  • I read the message three times and put the phone face down.
  • The bus came. I let it go.
Landing an ending
  • Tomorrow I will tell her. Probably.
  • Nothing had changed, and everything had.
  • I closed the door quietly, which is not how I usually close doors.

docs.title: Show it, do not label it
docs.text:
The quickest way to lift a creative text out of the middle band is to stop naming feelings.

Instead of Try I was very angry
  • I heard my own voice go flat
  • I folded the letter along its old creases, again and again
She was nervous
  • She checked the time twice in a minute
  • Her tea went cold beside her
It was a sad moment
  • Nobody moved to turn the light on
  • He kept talking about the weather

docs.title: Checklist for a creative text
docs.text:
• Am I writing the form the task asked for?
  • Is the moment fixed: exactly when does this happen?
  • Does everything my character says fit what they could know then?
  • Does anything I invented contradict the source?
  • Have I anchored the text in the original at least twice?
  • Is the voice the character's rather than mine?
  • Have I shown at least two feelings instead of naming them?
  • Does it have three beats: situation, turn, landing?
  • Have I revised for range as well as for correctness?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing a summary of the extract with "Dear diary" in front of it
  • Letting the character know something they only learn later in the text, or something only the narrator knows
  • Naming feelings instead of showing them: sad, angry, happy, nervous
  • Dropping the register: a nineteenth-century character using contemporary slang
  • Treating creative as a licence for careless English. Lexis and grammar are marked here exactly as they are in an analysis
  • Choosing this option in the examination because it looks shorter. It is not

See also: Written text types · How to write a comment · Exams & grading

docs.title: How to write a discussion essay
docs.text:
At a glance

Purpose Weigh both sides of an issue and reach a reasoned verdict Structure Introduction → arguments for and against → conclusion with your position Register & voice Neutral to formal, mostly neutral perspective, first person in the conclusion, simple present Length As set by the task, typically 300 to 400 words Watch out Your own opinion belongs in the conclusion, not earlier. Within each side: weakest argument first, strongest last

Operators for this task type:

Operator Example task discuss — most common, remember this one Should schools provide moral guidance? Discuss. (Abitur 2008) assess Assess the effectiveness of what authorities can do to change people's behaviour in order to deal with the problems of climate change. (Abitur 2023) evaluate Explain the concept of 'Britishness' by evaluating the validity of at least two of the given statements about the United Kingdom. (Abitur 2007)

See Operators.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Outline first. List the main pro and contra points before writing a single sentence. Pick the two or three strongest on each side.
  2. Write the introduction. Present the issue, give the background a reader needs, and define terms you will use. A one-sentence preview of how the essay is organized helps the reader follow you.

  3. Write the body. Two workable patterns:

    • Block pattern: all arguments for one side, then all arguments for the other.
    • Ping-pong pattern: point by point, each argument directly followed by its counterpart.

    Choose one and stay with it. In both patterns, move from the weakest argument to the strongest.

  4. Support every argument. Claim → reason → example. An argument without support is just an assertion.

  5. Conclude with a verdict. Weigh the two sides against each other and state which one convinces you more, and why. This is the only place for your opinion.

docs.text:
Purpose Phrases Introducing the issue
  • The question of whether … has been widely debated.
  • … is a controversial issue because …
  • Opinions on … differ sharply.
One side
  • Supporters argue that …
  • The strongest argument in favour is …
  • Those in favour point to …
The other side
  • Opponents point out that …
  • On the other hand, …
  • However, it can be argued that …
  • A serious objection is that …
Weighing up
  • Weighing the arguments, …
  • While … is a valid point, … carries more weight because …

Concluding
