docs.title: Checklist for a discussion essay
docs.text:
• Both sides represented with supported arguments?
  • One clear pattern (block or ping-pong) throughout?
  • Arguments ordered weakest to strongest?
  • Opinion only in the conclusion?
  • Conclusion actually weighs the sides instead of just repeating them?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Presenting one side so weakly that the "discussion" is really a comment
  • Revealing your opinion in the introduction
  • Jumping between the block and ping-pong patterns
  • A conclusion that says "both sides have good points" without a verdict

docs.title: How to write a mediation
docs.text:
At a glance

Purpose Transfer the content a specific addressee needs from a German text into English. Not a translation Structure The structure of the required text type: email, article, blog post, letter, report Register & voice Set by addressee and text type. Name your source. No opinion, no additions Length As set by the task. Class rule of thumb: about one quarter of the source. In the final examination the source is max. 650 words Watch out The task decides what is relevant, not the text. Never translate word for word, and never let German sentence patterns through

Operators for this task type: mediation itself is not set by one operator, the addressee and text type do that. The instruction for what to transfer rotates between these:

Operator Example task summarize / sum up — most common, remember this one Write a summary in English of what the following text says about children's values. (Abitur 2011) outline Outline what CityTrees are and why they might be interesting for big cities. (Abitur 2019) present Write an article for this website in which you present "Lieferrad DA". (Abitur 2023)

All of these ask for a concise account of the main points as the task specifies them. Where your addressee does not know a German institution or custom, you are expected to explain it.

See Operators.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Read the task first, then the text. The task tells you the purpose, the addressee and the text type. Read the German text with the task in mind: what does this addressee need?
  2. Get an overview (first reading). What is the topic, what are the core statements?
  3. Read closely (second reading). Work through the text section by section. Mark the statements that answer the task; cross out examples and details that do not.
  4. Order the information. Group related points and put them in a logical order. You do not have to follow the structure of the German text.

  5. Write the mediation.

    • Opening: name the source (title, author, publication, date) and the topic, adapted to your text type. An email starts with a greeting and a reason for writing.
    • Body: neutral register, no colloquial language, no personal opinion. Do not translate German idioms word by word; find an English way to say the same thing.
    • Ending: round the text off according to its type. An email needs a closing formula; a summary-style mediation simply ends with the last point.

  6. Revise. Compare against the task, check the word count, correct the language.

docs.text:
Purpose Phrases Referring to the source
  • The article "…" from … deals with …
  • According to an article published in … on …, …
  • As … explains in …, …
Reporting content
  • The author explains that …
  • As the text points out, …
  • It is reported that …
  • The article goes on to describe …
Explaining a German term
  • … , which is roughly the German equivalent of …
  • … , a German concept meaning …
  • In Germany, … is organized by …
  • Unlike in the UK, …
Email or letter frame
  • I am writing to you because …
  • I came across an article that might interest you.
  • I hope this helps. Let me know if you have any questions.
Article or website frame
  • If you are looking for an example from Germany, look at …
  • This is how it works in practice: …
  • What makes the idea work is …

docs.title: Checklist for a mediation
docs.text:
• All aspects of the task covered, and only those?
  • Text type conventions met (greeting, closing, headline …)?
  • Word limit kept?
  • Source named in the opening?
  • No literal translations of German idioms or sentence patterns?
  • No own opinion added?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Translating sentence by sentence; the result sounds German and is far too long
  • Including every detail instead of selecting for the task
  • Forgetting the addressee: an email to a friend does not sound like an essay
  • False friends (e.g. aktuell ≠ actual, Chef ≠ chef, eventuell ≠ eventually)

docs.title: How to write a speech
docs.text:
At a glance

Purpose Move an audience towards one message: to think, feel or do something Structure Attention-grabbing opening → body with about three points → memorable ending Register & voice Neutral to formal, first person, address the audience directly with we, us, you Length As set by the task. Spoken delivery: roughly 130 words per minute Watch out Write for the ear, not the eye. Rhetorical devices must serve the message, not decorate it

Operators for this task type: a speech is the single most requested text type on the whole exam, remember that.

Operator Example task write (a speech) Write a speech for this conference reflecting on the relevance of historical events. (Abitur 2010) write … comment (on) Write the script of your speech in which you comment on this attitude towards literature. (Abitur 2021)

write sets the format, it is often combined with a second operator (usually comment) that sets what the speech has to argue. See Operators.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Find your purpose. What should the audience think, feel or do after your speech? Write that down in one sentence; it is your thesis.
  2. Know your audience. Who are they, what do they care about, what do they already know? This decides your examples, your register and your opening.
  3. Grab attention at the start. Options: a rhetorical question, a surprising fact, a short anecdote, a provocative statement. Then state your topic and why it matters to this audience.
  4. Build the body. About three main points, each supported by a reason and a vivid example. Order them so the strongest comes last. Signal every transition ("This brings me to …").
  5. Make it persuasive. Sound arguments first (logos), then add emotional appeal (pathos) and credibility (ethos). Devices that work in speeches: anaphora, rule of three, inclusive pronouns, contrast, imagery. See stylistic devices.
  6. End strongly. Return to your opening, summarize your message in one sharp sentence, and close with an appeal or a thought the audience takes home.

docs.text:
Purpose Phrases Opening
  • Have you ever wondered … ?
  • Imagine for a moment that …
  • Let me start with a simple fact: …
  • Two years ago, I …
Addressing the audience
  • Ladies and gentlemen, …
  • Fellow students, …
  • All of us know …
  • You and I have both …
Structuring
  • Let me make three points.
  • This brings me to my second point.
  • And that is precisely why …
  • So where does that leave us?
Involving the audience
  • We all know the feeling.
  • Ask yourselves: …
  • Together, we can …
  • Put yourself in their position.
Closing
  • So let us …
  • The choice is ours.
  • If you remember one thing from today, let it be this: …
  • Thank you.

docs.title: Checklist for a speech
docs.text:
• One clear message, stated and repeated?
  • Opening that actually grabs attention?
  • About three supported points with signalled transitions?
  • Audience addressed and included throughout?
  • At least three rhetorical devices used deliberately?
  • Strong closing line?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing an essay and reading it out: no address, no "we", long written-style sentences
  • Cramming in too many points instead of developing three
  • Devices used at random rather than where they support the message
  • A closing that trails off ("…and that's why I think it's important.")

docs.title: How to write an outline or summary
docs.text:
At a glance

Purpose Give a concise account of the main points of a text, as the task specifies, so that someone who has not read it understands it Structure Introductory sentence → key points in a logical order → (optional) closing sentence Register & voice Neutral to formal, neutral point of view, simple present, reported speech where needed Length As set by the task. Class rule of thumb: about one third of the original Watch out Class rule of thumb: no more than four consecutive words from the source. Select by the task, then group and abstract. No examples, no quotations, no opinion

Operators for this task type: outline, summarize and sum up are one operator in the exam: a concise account of the main points as the task specifies them.

Operator Example task outline — most common, remember this one Outline the information given on Dell and his family. (Abitur 2020) summarize / sum up Sum up what you learn about the protagonist. (Abitur 2007)

Look at what the examples ask for. Not the whole text, but the information on Dell and his family, or what you learn about the protagonist. A task like this is not "write a summary of the text". The task names the angle, and everything that does not belong to it stays out.

See Operators.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Read the task first, then the text twice. The task names the aspect you are after. Read once for the general idea, then closely with that aspect in mind. Look up words you need for understanding.
  2. Mark the key statements. Only those that answer the task. Ignore examples, figures, anecdotes and repetitions.
  3. Group and abstract. Combine related points under one higher-level statement and write that statement, not the details beneath it. Stay one step above the text. You may reorder, you do not have to follow the structure of the original.
  4. Write the introductory sentence. One neutral sentence with author, title, place and date of publication, text type and main topic.
  5. Write the body. Connect the key points with linking words. Use reporting verbs to keep the distance to the text.
  6. Revise. Check tense, the four-word rule of thumb and whether someone who has not read the text would understand your account.

docs.title: Useful phrases
docs.text:
Purpose Phrases Introductory sentence
  • The article "…" by …, published in … on …, deals with …
  • The short story "…" by … (…) describes …
  • In the text "…", … examines the question of …
Reporting the author's points
  • The author states / points out / argues that …
  • The author claims / criticizes / emphasizes that …
  • It is reported that …
  • According to the text, …
Structuring
  • First, the author …
  • He then goes on to …
  • In the second part, the focus shifts to …
  • The author concludes by …
Referring back
  • According to the author, …
  • In the author's view, …
  • As mentioned above, …

More under Useful phrases for writing.

docs.title: Checklist for an outline or summary
docs.text:
• Only what the task asks for, nothing else from the text?
  • Introductory sentence complete (author, title, place and date, text type, topic)?
  • Simple present throughout?
  • Details grouped under higher-level statements instead of retold one by one?
  • Own words, no copied phrases from the text?
  • No examples, no quotes, no opinion?
  • Understandable without the original text?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Summarizing the whole text although the task names one aspect
  • Staying so close to the text that the account reads like a shortened copy
  • Copying whole phrases from the text instead of paraphrasing
  • Drifting into past tense halfway through
  • Retelling every detail instead of selecting key statements
  • Smuggling in your own opinion; that belongs in a comment, not in an outline or summary
